743.title: Arjuna bows before the bow
743.hook: a disguised archer walks around the bow and bows before he lifts it
743.carry: pradakshina: honor what's sacred before you begin
743.howItsDone: Walking around something sacred to honor it, pradakshina, is part of Hindu worship: people walk around temple shrines, sacred trees and the wedding fire, keeping them on their right.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Karna at the bow, one sentence from the princess, and a glance at the sun. Your line: Surya, the sun, sees what the arena can't.
screen: `SURYA, THE SUN, SEES WHAT THE ARENA CAN'T.`

segments.voice: The kings have failed. Karna has put down the bow. The arena goes quiet. From the benches where the brahmins sit, a young man stands up, dressed like any brahmin student. The brahmins around him murmur. Some are alarmed: where famous kings have failed, what's a brahmin going to do, except make the rest of us look foolish? Others look at his arms and the way he carries himself, and say: let him go.
screen: `THE ARENA GOES QUIET.` → `A BRAHMIN STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: It's Arjuna, in disguise. He walks up to the bow and around it, the text says, bows his head to Shiva, the giver of boons, and remembers Krishna. Then he picks it up. In a moment the bow is strung. He shoots, and the mark falls to the ground. The arena erupts. Flowers fall from the sky, the text says, and Draupadi comes toward him and places her garland on him. The kings are furious that a nameless brahmin has taken the prize, and they rise to fight; Bhima tears up a tree and stands beside his brother. But go back to that pause before the bow. The best archer alive, in front of every king, stops, walks around the thing he's about to use, and bows. Hindus still do exactly this. Walking around something holy, keeping it on your right, is called pradakshina: people circle the shrine at a temple, the tulsi plant at home, and at a wedding the couple circle the sacred fire. And the bow before the work is everywhere: a dancer touches the floor before she dances, a musician touches the instrument, a child who drops a book touches it, then touches their forehead. The teaching underneath: what you're about to use isn't only a tool. Honor first, then act. Arjuna's strength comes after his bow.
screen: `HE WALKS AROUND THE BOW AND BOWS.` · `THE MARK FALLS.` · `DRAUPADI'S GARLAND.` · `PRADAKSHINA: CIRCLE WHAT'S HOLY.` · then, large: `HONOR FIRST, THEN ACT.`

segments.voice: Before something today asks a lot of you, do what Arjuna did, and what Hindu families do every day. Stop in front of it. If you pray, fold your hands and remember God by whatever name your family uses; if there's a home shrine or a tulsi plant nearby, some families walk around it once, keeping it on the right. If you don't pray, simply stand still and bow your head to the work for one slow breath. Then begin.
Draupadi's swayamvara, the bride's own choosing. Today, a disguised archer honors the bow before he lifts it, and wins.
Your line: pradakshina: honor what's sacred before you begin. Arjuna bowed first; the strength came after. Until tomorrow.

744.title: Kunti's word at the door
744.hook: two brothers come home with a princess, and their mother answers without looking
744.carry: satya: even a careless word is kept true
744.howItsDone: Bhiksha, food given as alms, is part of Hindu religious life: renunciants, and in some traditions students, receive food from householders, which is why the brothers, dressed as brahmins, call what they bring home alms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, at Draupadi's swayamvara, Arjuna walked around the bow and bowed before he lifted it. Your line was pradakshina: honor what's sacred before you begin.

Someone in the crowd has worked it out. While the kings fight, Krishna watches the brahmin with the bow and the giant with the tree, and turns to his brother Balarama. That one with the tree, he says, is Bhima. The archer is Arjuna. They didn't die in the fire. Meanwhile, at the potter's house where the family is staying, Kunti waits. It's late, and her sons haven't come back.

Bhima and Arjuna come to the door with Draupadi. They're living as brahmins, on alms, so they call in: look, we've brought alms. And Kunti, inside, without looking up, answers the way a mother might: share it, all of you. Then she sees who's standing there. A princess, not a bowl of rice. What have I said, Kunti cries, the text says. Why doesn't she just say oops? Because in the Mahabharata, satya, truthfulness, sits near the heart of dharma, and a spoken word is something you keep. Kunti didn't mean it, and still she won't let her word go false. But she doesn't force it, either. She takes Draupadi by the hand, goes to Yudhishthira, and asks how her word can stay true without wrong being done to the princess. Truth, held with care. Yudhishthira offers Draupadi to Arjuna, who won her; Arjuna says the eldest should marry first. Then Yudhishthira, remembering words Vyasa once spoke and fearing his brothers could be divided, says she'll be the wife of all. The Bhagavad Gita, later in this same epic, names the discipline of speech: words that are true, kind and helpful, that cause no one distress. Hindu grandmothers teach it more simply: don't say what you don't mean, because words count. And then Krishna arrives at the potter's door, and bows at Yudhishthira's feet.

745.title: Dharma is subtle
745.hook: a king objects to his daughter's marriage, and the answer is that dharma is subtle
745.carry: dharma is subtle: hard cases need honest questions
745.tomorrow: Fear not: Maya spared from the fire
745.howItsDone: Draupadi's marriage is discussed in Hindu teaching and retelling; some retellings lean on Vyasa's account of her past life, and some modern novels tell the whole Mahabharata from Draupadi's side.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi's swayamvara came home: Kunti's word, given without looking, and kept with care. Your line was satya: even a careless word is kept true.

Drupada has a problem. His daughter was won by a brahmin no one could name, and now he learns who the man really is: Arjuna, alive, the one he'd hoped for from the start. Good news. Then Yudhishthira tells him the rest. Draupadi will be the wife of all five brothers. Drupada objects at once. One woman with many husbands, he says, is not the way of the Vedas or of custom. How can you, who know what's right, propose this?

Yudhishthira answers carefully. Dharma is subtle, he says, and its path is hard to see. He follows where those before him walked, and his mother has spoken. Then Vyasa arrives, and Drupada asks him directly: is this right, or not? Vyasa takes Drupada aside and tells him a story. In an earlier life, your daughter was a sage's daughter who couldn't find a husband. She practiced hard austerities, and Shiva came to grant her a wish. Give me a husband, she asked, again and again. And Shiva told her: since you asked more than once, in another birth you'll have more than one husband. Vyasa tells a second story too, of the brothers as gods born on earth, and Drupada is persuaded. Now the teaching, in Yudhishthira's first words: dharma is subtle. The Mahabharata says it again and again; it's one of the epic's big ideas. Dharma, the right way, isn't always a rule you look up. Sometimes good rules pull against each other: a mother's word, a father's custom, brothers who mustn't be divided. So the poem doesn't hide the hard case. It lets Drupada object out loud that this isn't the custom, and it gives four reasons, not one. And Draupadi herself says almost nothing here; her voice comes later, and it's fierce. Hindus have argued over this marriage ever since. That's how the epic teaches: with cases hard enough to make you ask.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a hard question in your own family or faith, one where two good things pull against each other. Don't solve it. Hold both sides, the way the poem holds Drupada's objection and Yudhishthira's answer, and then ask who hasn't been heard yet. If you pray, ask for clear sight; if you don't, just let the question stay open a little longer.
Draupadi's swayamvara. Its last piece: Drupada's objection, Yudhishthira's answer, and Vyasa's story of a wish asked more than once.
Your line: dharma is subtle: hard cases need honest questions. Four answers, and the poem still lets you ask. That's the swayamvara, start to finish.

746.title: Fear not: Maya spared from the fire
746.hook: a builder runs out of a burning forest, and Arjuna says: don't be afraid
746.carry: abhaya: protect the one who asks for refuge
746.howItsDone: The raised open palm on many Hindu murtis is the abhaya mudra, the gesture that says 'fear not'. Hindu tradition places the Pandavas' city of Indraprastha near present-day Delhi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi's swayamvara ended in a wedding, after Drupada's objection and Vyasa's story. Your line was dharma is subtle: hard cases need honest questions.

A forest is on fire, and a man runs out of it. He's Maya, an asura and a master builder, with the flames at his back. Krishna raises his discus. Maya cries out to Arjuna to save him, and Arjuna answers: don't be afraid. Those words save his life. And the next book of the Mahabharata, the Sabha Parva, the book of the hall, opens with the man they saved.
screen: `A FOREST ON FIRE.` → `MAYA CRIES OUT.` → `DON'T BE AFRAID.`

segments.voice: First, how the family got here. After the wedding, the Pandavas go back to Hastinapura. Dhritarashtra gives them half the kingdom, the wild half, and there they build a city, Indraprastha. Then Krishna and Arjuna help the fire god Agni burn the Khandava forest, guarding its edges so nothing escapes. It's a hard chapter: the text names only a handful who survive. Maya is one, because of one sentence. Don't be afraid. And Krishna stays his hand. Those words are one of the great gifts in Hindu dharma, and the gift has a name: abhaya, fearlessness, the gift of safety to someone who comes asking for refuge. In the epics, protecting the one who asks for shelter is counted a high duty, even when he's from the enemy's side; in the Ramayana, Rama takes in Ravana's own brother when he comes for refuge. And you've seen abhaya. On many Hindu images, Ganesha, Durga, Shiva as the dancer, one hand is raised, palm open, facing you. It doesn't mean stop. It's the abhaya mudra: don't be afraid. Many Hindus read it two ways: a promise from God to you, and a job for you. The worried cousin who needs a couch, the classmate nobody sits with: abhaya means you say 'you're safe here' first and ask questions later. Then Maya, safe, wants to repay Arjuna. Arjuna won't take anything; in paraphrase, be a friend to me. So Krishna asks for a gift for someone else: build a hall for Yudhishthira, one no one could copy. That's this stretch's word, sabha: a hall, and the assembly that meets in it.
screen: `INDRAPRASTHA AND THE KHANDAVA FIRE.` · `ABHAYA: DON'T BE AFRAID.` · `SHELTER FOR THE ONE WHO ASKS.` · `THE RAISED OPEN PALM.` · then, large: `A HALL FOR YUDHISHTHIRA.`

segments.voice: Raise your right hand, palm open and facing out, the way it's raised on so many Hindu images. Hold it there for a few breaths, and bring to mind someone who's afraid right now. If you pray, ask God to be their shelter; if you don't, simply wish them safety. Then lower your hand and think of one way you could be someone's 'don't be afraid' this week.
Sabha. A hall, and the assembly that gathers in it. Today, the hall at Indraprastha is promised by a builder who heard Arjuna say: don't be afraid.
Your line: abhaya: protect the one who asks for refuge. One raised hand says it. See you tomorrow.

747.title: Griha pravesha: the hall opens
747.hook: Maya goes north for his materials, comes back with a mace and a conch, and builds a hall with a pool that looks like floor
747.carry: griha pravesha: a new home opens by feeding people
747.howItsDone: Moving into a new home, Hindu families often hold a griha pravesha, a house-entering ceremony: a puja, often to Ganesha first, milk boiled until it overflows in many families, and a meal shared with guests before the family settles in.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna told a builder in a burning forest, don't be afraid, and a sabha was promised. Your line was abhaya: protect the one who asks for refuge.

Before Maya lays a single stone, he leaves. He goes north, past Kailasa, the text says, to a lake called Bindu, where he'd stored treasures long before. He comes back carrying gifts: a heavy mace bound in gold for Bhima, a conch called Devadatta, with a sound that carries, for Arjuna, and crystal and jewels and everything a hall like no other would need. Only then does he start building.
screen: `NORTH, PAST KAILASA.` → `A MACE FOR BHIMA.` → `A CONCH FOR ARJUNA.`

segments.voice: The text spends a long time on this hall. Walls that shine like the sun. Trees in bloom inside, and a cool breeze. In the middle, a pool: lotuses on the water, crystal steps going down. The water was so still and clear that kings who came to see it, the text says, took it for solid floor, and fell in. Hold onto that pool; this serial will come back to it. Now watch what Yudhishthira does before he steps inside. He feeds a great crowd of brahmanas: rice and ghee, honey, fruit. He gives away cows. There's music, there are offerings, and only after all that does he enter. Hindu families still open a home this way. It's called griha pravesha, entering the house. You don't just carry in the boxes. There's a puja, often to Ganesha first; many families boil milk until it spills over, a sign of plenty; and there's food, lots of it, for the priest, the relatives, the neighbors, before anyone sleeps there. Behind it is anna dana, the gift of food, which Hindus often call one of the greatest gifts there is. A home, or a king's hall, begins as a place where people were fed. Then the hall fills. Sages come, kings come, singers come. That's the other half of the word sabha: the gathering. A sabha with no one in it is only a building.
screen: `A HALL LIKE NO OTHER.` · `A POOL THAT LOOKS LIKE FLOOR.` · `FEED THEM FIRST, THEN ENTER.` · `GRIHA PRAVESHA: ENTERING THE HOME.` · then, large: `A HOME BEGINS WHERE PEOPLE WERE FED.`

segments.voice: Next time you eat today, do what many Hindus do before the first bite: offer it first, a moment of thanks, or a little set aside for God. If you don't pray, let the pause be your thanks. Then bring to mind one person you could feed this week, a guest, a neighbor, a friend who's had a long day, and picture setting the plate in front of them.
Sabha. A hall, and the assembly that meets in it. Maya's hall at Indraprastha, opened the way Hindu homes still open: by feeding people first.
Your line: griha pravesha: a new home opens by feeding people. The people make it a sabha. Day seven hundred forty-seven, done.

748.title: Narada asks about the people
748.hook: Narada walks into the new hall and, instead of praising it, starts asking the king questions
748.carry: rajadharma: a leader's duty is the people's welfare
748.howItsDone: Narada's questions are read in Hindu tradition as a lesson in how to rule well, and they're often retold alongside the Mahabharata's other teachings on a king's duty, or rajadharma.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sabha opened by feeding a crowd, with a pool so clear that kings fell in. Your line was griha pravesha: a new home opens by feeding people.

A visitor walks into the new hall at Indraprastha and doesn't say a word about the building. Yudhishthira sits with his brothers, sages and kings around him. Then Narada comes in, the wandering sage, with other rishis behind him. The Pandavas stand, bow, and give him a seat. And Narada, looking at the king who owns this wonder, begins to ask him questions. Not about the crystal. About the kingdom.
screen: `NARADA ARRIVES.` → `A SEAT FOR THE SAGE.` → `QUESTIONS, NOT PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Narada's questions run on and on, and in the Sanskrit they lean on a small word, kaccit. It asks while hoping the answer is yes, something like: I hope that you are. A few, in paraphrase. Do you divide your time well between what's right, what's useful, and what's enjoyable? Are your ministers honest, and do they keep your counsel? Do your soldiers get their pay and food on time? Do you look after the families of men who died serving you? Do farmers have seed and food when they need it, and are there tanks and lakes, so farming doesn't hang on the rain alone? Notice where these go. The hall is right there, shining. Narada's eyes go past it, to a soldier's widow, a farmer waiting for rain. This has a name in Hindu teaching: rajadharma, the dharma of a king. The Mahabharata comes back to it again and again, and its answer is steady: the ruler is there for the people, not the people for the ruler. A king in a crystal hall whose soldiers go unpaid has failed his dharma, however fine the hall. And the tone matters too. Kaccit doesn't accuse. It says, I hope this is so, and leaves room for the king to answer, and to fix what isn't so yet. Yudhishthira bows and says he'll do what's been asked. The building is the occasion. The people are the point.
screen: `KACCIT: I HOPE THAT YOU ARE.` · `SOLDIERS, WIDOWS, FARMERS.` · `RAJADHARMA: THE DUTY OF A KING.` · `ASKED IN HOPE, NOT ACCUSATION.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE ARE THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Choose one place where other people depend on you: a household, a team, a class, a friendship. Ask it one question the way Narada asks a king, beginning with I hope: I hope the people here are fed, I hope someone is being heard. If you pray, hold those people before God as you ask; if you don't, just let the answer come, and notice what the question turns up.
Sabha. The hall where a king sits to hear his people. Today, Narada fills it with questions about rajadharma, each one asked in hope.
Your line: rajadharma: a leader's duty is the people's welfare. Narada asked about people, not crystal. Until tomorrow.

749.title: Narada and the guardians' halls
749.hook: Yudhishthira asks Narada if he's ever seen a hall like this, and Narada describes the halls of the gods
749.carry: lokapalas: every direction has a guardian
749.howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, Indra (east), Yama (south), Varuna (west) and Kubera (north) are among the guardians of the directions, the lokapalas or dikpalas, and their images are carved at their directions on the walls of some temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Narada in the sabha, asking about soldiers, farmers and widows. Your line was rajadharma: a leader's duty is the people's welfare.

It's a very human question. The questions are over, the king has promised to do better, and then Yudhishthira asks Narada something else. You've traveled through every world, he says. Have you ever seen a hall like this one, or a better one? He's sitting in the hall Maya built; of course he wants to know. And Narada's answer is careful. Among humans, he says, never. But there are other halls.
screen: `HAVE YOU SEEN A HALL LIKE THIS?` → `AMONG HUMANS, NEVER.` → `BUT THERE ARE OTHER HALLS.`

segments.voice: Then Narada describes them, one after another, the halls of the gods. The hall of Indra, king of the gods. Of Yama, lord of the dead. Of Varuna, out among the waters. Of Kubera, lord of wealth. And the hall of Brahma, the creator, which Narada says can't be properly described at all, because its form keeps changing. Listen to how he describes them. He tells what they're made of and how bright they are, but mostly he lists who sits there: sages, kings of old, ancestors, rivers and mountains in person. Each hall is known by its gathering, the word sabha again. And notice whose halls these are. Indra, Yama, Varuna, Kubera: in Hindu tradition they're lokapalas, guardians of the world, and each keeps a direction. Indra the east, where the sun rises. Yama the south. Varuna the west. Kubera the north. That's why some Hindu temples carve them on their outer walls, facing their directions: the holy place stands inside a world watched on every side. So Narada's answer doesn't flatter Yudhishthira, and it doesn't scold him. Nothing among humans matches your hall, he says, and then shows him the larger world it stands in, guarded in every direction, and beyond it a hall no words can hold. Many teachers read it as a gentle lesson in humility. It's also a setup. In Yama's hall, among the kings who've died, is someone Yudhishthira would know.
screen: `INDRA, YAMA, VARUNA, KUBERA.` · `EACH HALL KNOWN BY WHO SITS THERE.` · `LOKAPALAS: A GUARDIAN FOR EACH DIRECTION.` · `BRAHMA'S HALL KEEPS CHANGING.` · then, large: `NOTHING LIKE IT ON EARTH. HERE IS THE SKY.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and turn slowly to each direction: east, south, west, north. In each one, think of what lies that way, a street, a city, someone you love. Some Hindu prayers greet each direction in turn. If you pray, ask God to watch over that side of your world; if you don't, simply notice that your room sits inside something much bigger, on every side.
Sabha. A hall, and its assembly. Today, Narada's tour of the halls of the gods, the guardians of the directions, each hall known by who sits in it.
Your line: lokapalas: every direction has a guardian. Narada gave pride company, not a scolding. That's the week.
